parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Choose the portfolio before the platform
parts.body:
An 18-month transformation plan starts with a small set of business outcomes and the uses that could produce them. For each candidate, estimate value against a baseline, feasibility, data readiness, consequence of failure, and the business owner's willingness to change the workflow. Select a first use whose evidence can be collected. Explain which promising use is deferred and why.

Draw a value-versus-readiness chart for discussion, but retain the underlying figures and judgments. A high-value use with uncertain data rights may justify a short discovery investment rather than a full build. A modest internal use may earn an early slot because it tests shared evaluation and monitoring capability. Portfolio sequencing should reveal what the organization needs to learn, not reward a slide with the most ambitious forecast.

Define gates for discovery, pilot, and scale. Discovery checks rights and baseline; pilot tests quality, usage, unit economics, and controls on representative cases; scale requires a named operating owner and support model. Set thresholds appropriate to consequences and record who can approve or pause each stage.

example.title: A portfolio choice
example.body: The hypothetical insurer funds internal claims drafting first, investigates document retrieval rights in parallel, and defers automated coverage recommendations. The first use has a human reviewer and measurable draft time; the deferred use needs deeper risk and data assessment.

exercise.title: Rank four uses
exercise.body: Score four cases for expected value, evidence quality, data readiness, consequence of error, and workflow owner. Choose two to fund and one to defer. Explain a case where a lower value use should go first.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: Map, Measure, Manage

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Sequence dependencies and architecture
parts.body:
Build the roadmap backward from each release condition. A claims drafting assistant may need permission-aware retrieval, clean source documents, identity integration, audit records, evaluation cases, human review, and an incident path. Place those dependencies before the launch they enable. Reuse a shared capability only when its service owner, cost, access model, and change process are clear. Avoid declaring one platform mandatory for every use.

Draw the data path from source to user: where records are stored, what is retrieved, what goes to a model or vendor, what is logged, and what a reviewer sees. Mark trust boundaries and the owner of each component. Include a fallback for outage or unacceptable answers. If the architecture sends personal information to a third party, privacy, security, and procurement reviews become explicit prerequisites.

Use four decision windows in the illustrative 18-month plan. Months 0–3 validate data rights, baseline, and architecture and authorize or refuse a pilot. Months 4–6 test a supervised workflow with representative cases, unit economics, and a release gate. Months 7–12 expand only to another team if the pilot passes, build support and monitoring capacity, and reassess the deferred use. Months 13–18 decide whether measured value warrants regional expansion, reinvestment, or retirement. Each window has a funding cap, owner, evidence packet, and stop route. If an early test fails, move the downstream date and show the avoidable cost.

example.title: A worked sequence with gates
example.body: Fictional Northlake Mutual, months 0–3: claims VP approves CAD 60,000 discovery only; data owner confirms permissions on 100 sampled records, IT diagrams role-based retrieval, and finance measures baseline time and rework. Gate A requires approved purpose and records, a measured baseline, and a supervised workflow. Months 4–6: if A passes, fund a capped internal pilot; evaluation lead labels 150 cases, privacy and security sign their reviews, and claims VP approves release after a representative quality test. Gate B requires no deterioration in reopened cases, positive net unit value, and an incident fallback. Months 7–12: expand to another team only if B passes. Months 13–18: consider EU scope only after new jurisdiction, data, and language reviews. All caps and case counts are illustrative.

exercise.title: Trace one use end to end
exercise.body: Draw source, permissions, retrieval, model, output, reviewer, logging, and fallback. Put a person and evidence item at each release dependency. Move any capability scheduled after launch to the point where it is actually needed.

sources: OPC Canada: assessing third-party service providers

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Fund value, controls, and people together
parts.body:
A credible budget covers more than model usage. Include data work, integration, vendor or compute charges, evaluation, security and privacy review, support, training, change management, and contingency. Give a cost range, funding by stage, and owner. Benefits should be net of rework and operating cost; distinguish capacity released from cash saved. An hour freed is valuable, but it is not automatically a payroll reduction.

Describe the operating model beside the budget. The business executive owns the outcome and workflow. The CAIO coordinates portfolio standards and evidence. CIO and engineering own technology service, CISO owns security controls, privacy and legal own their reviews, and finance tests economics. Actual authority follows the organization's charter. Identify the team that will maintain evaluation cases, respond to incidents, and retrain users when a system changes.

For Canada and the EU, add jurisdiction-specific review tasks to the plan rather than a generic global compliance box. The EU AI Act's classification and duties depend on the use and role; Canadian privacy obligations depend on the governing regime and purpose. Counsel must verify obligations and current dates at each relevant release gate.

example.title: A financial scenario with a downside
example.body: Fictional annual steady-state case: 40,000 eligible claims, 50% adoption, six minutes of net time saved per assisted claim, CAD 40 per usable hour, CAD 60,000 fixed operating cost, and CAD 1.50 variable cost per assisted claim. Modeled capacity value is 20,000 × 6/60 × CAD 40 = CAD 80,000; run cost is CAD 60,000 + CAD 30,000, so net capacity value is negative CAD 10,000 before setup. At 70% adoption, value is CAD 112,000 and run cost CAD 102,000, leaving CAD 10,000 before setup. Neither is cash savings absent an actual staffing or redeployment decision. Discovery and pilot caps are separate, illustrative investments. Finance should refuse scale on this value case alone unless measured benefits or costs change.

exercise.title: Build the finance page
exercise.body: For one use, estimate setup and annual run costs, low/base/high volume, correction effort, net unit benefit, and break-even point. Show the treatment of released staff time. Name the budget owner and the condition for the next funding tranche.

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Make the plan executable
parts.body:
Now assemble one decision packet: strategic thesis, prioritized portfolio, 18-month dependency roadmap, architecture, operating model, risk register, budget scenarios, workforce changes, scorecard, and decision calendar. Each section should agree with the others. If the scorecard measures a benefit the budget never forecasts, reconcile it. If a use needs a data right not yet established, put that validation before its release and mark funding conditional.

Test the highest-priority use from end to end. Can you identify its business owner, baseline, permitted data, evaluation set, quality threshold, security and privacy reviewers, pilot cap, launch authority, monitoring signal, incident route, and retirement trigger? A missing link is a useful finding, not a reason to invent certainty. Assign the gap an owner and date.

Ask someone unfamiliar with your plan to find the first three decisions and their evidence. Rework a schedule that is only a list of activities. An executive should see where money can be stopped or redirected as learning arrives.

example.title: A failed gate changes funding and dates
example.body: At month three, Northlake Mutual's data owner finds only 45 of 100 sampled records have clear retrieval rights, below the planned 80 of 100 needed for the pilot design. The claims VP declines the CAD 300,000 pilot tranche, authorizes up to CAD 25,000 from the unused discovery contingency for rights remediation and approved de-identified tests, and moves the earliest real-data pilot decision to month five. Privacy counsel reviews the revised purpose and records; finance removes months 7–12 capacity benefit from the forecast. EU expansion is deferred until the Canadian design and its evidence are stable. All figures are fictional and the 80% gate is a case-specific choice.

exercise.title: Perform a traceability review
exercise.body: Follow the top use through ten items: owner, baseline, rights, architecture, evaluation, control review, budget, gate, monitoring, and stop rule. Mark each evidenced, assumed, or missing. Revise the plan until every missing item has a discovery step.

sources: OECD due diligence guidance for responsible AI
